Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 104, verses 1–9:

Makkan, and its verses are 9 [revealed after al-Qiyamah]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-hamz (the breaking, like al-hazm). Al-lamz is slandering. It is said: lamazahu and lahazahu, meaning he slandered him. The meaning is breaking people's honour, belittling them (ghadd minhum), backbiting them, and defaming them. [[The commentator's phrase "breaking people's honour and belittling them" is explained in al-Sihah: ghadda minhu means he lowered him, diminished him, and reduced his standing. (Gh.)]] [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning of al-humaza is one who frequently slanders people and disparages them..." Ahmad said: How excellent is the contrast between al-humaza al-lumaza and al-hutama. When He marked him with this trait in a form that indicates it is firmly rooted in him and entrenched in him, He followed the emphasis with His threat of the Fire, which He named al-Hutama because of what is cast into it. In specifying it He used an intensive form on the pattern of the form that contains the sin, so that there is equivalence between the sin and the recompense. Thus, the one who was accustomed to sin, his recompense is this al-Hutama, which is habitually crushing everything cast into it.]] The pattern fu'alah indicates that this is his habit, to which he has become accustomed. Similar are al-lu'nah (the curse) and al-du'hakah (the one who laughs much). He said:

"If I am absent, you are the one who slanders and backbites."

[[When you meet me, you grin at me from a distance, and when I am absent you are the backbiter who abundantly defames my honour.]]

This is by Ziyad al-A'jam. Al-shahth, with a fatha, means distance. Kathara 'an asnanihi means he showed his teeth in laughter and other things, but in the Arabic language this is known primarily for the first (laughter). Al-hamz is breaking, and al-lamz is slander. It is reported that a Bedouin was asked: "Does the mouse get broken (yahmizu)?" He said: "Yes, the cat breaks it," meaning it eats it. The al-hamiz here is the backbiter, the one who frequently backbites, who fills his mouth with what damages another's honour. Al-humazah is one who has made this a habit. Al-lamiz is one who attacks another with insults. Al-lumazah is one who has made this a habit. He means: when you meet me across the distance between us, you laugh at me, and when I am absent from you, you are the backbiter who abundantly defames my honour. It is also reported as "and if I am absent, you are the al-hamiz," in the passive form.

It is also read: "Woe to the al-humazah al-lumazah." And it is read: "Woe to every humazah lumazah," with a sukun on the mim, meaning the mocker who brings up outrageous things and jokes, so that he is laughed at and insulted. It is said that it was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose habit was backbiting and disparagement. It is said that it was about Umayyah ibn Khalaf. It is said that it was about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and his backbiting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and belittling him. It is permissible that the cause was specific while the threat is general, so that it encompasses everyone who engages in that ugly act, and so that it serves as an indirect rebuke to the one mentioned, since that is more effective in restraining him and more painful to him. Alladhi is a substitute for "every" (from kull), or it is in the accusative on the basis of censure. It is also read: jamma'a with the shaddah, which corresponds to his number. It is said 'addadahu means he made it a count for the calamities of time. It is also read: wa-'addadahu, meaning he gathered wealth, counted its amount and reckoned it. Or it means he gathered his wealth and the people who support him, from your saying: "So-and-so has a number and a band" when he has a large number of supporters and what they need. It is said that wa-'addadahu means wa-'adda-hu, with the idghām undone, like dannu akhlada-hu and khalladahu, which have the same meaning, meaning: wealth prolonged his hope, and far-reaching wishes gave him hope, until, because of his extreme heedlessness and long hope, he thinks his wealth has left him immortal in this world and that he will not die. Or it means he acts, through constructing buildings firmly with stone and brick, planting trees and cultivating the land, as one who thinks his wealth has kept him alive. Or it is an indirect reference to righteous deeds, and that it is these that cause their doer to abide in bliss, whereas wealth has not made anyone abide in anything.

It is reported that al-Akhnas had four thousand dinars. It is said ten thousand. From al-Hasan: he returned wealthy and said: "What do you say about thousands with which I did not ransom myself from a base person, nor did I show favour to a noble one?" He said: "But why?" He said: "Because of the calamity of the age, the harshness of the ruler, the misfortunes of time, and fear of poverty." He said: "Then you leave it to one who does not praise you, and you give back to one who does not excuse you."

Kalla (no indeed) is a rebuke to him for his assumption. It is read: la-yanbadhanna, meaning he and his wealth; la-yanbadhanna with the dhamma on the dhal, meaning he and his helpers. La-yanbadhanna fi al-hutamah, in the Fire, which by its nature crushes everything cast into it. It is said of a man who eats excessively: he is a hutamah. It is also read: al-hatimah, meaning that it enters their insides until it reaches their chests and rises over their hearts, which are the middle of the heart. Nothing in the human body is more delicate than the heart, and nothing more sensitive to pain from the slightest harm touching it. How much more so when the Fire of Hell rises over it and takes control of it. It is permissible that the hearts are singled out because they are the seats of disbelief, corrupt beliefs and evil intentions. The meaning of the Fire rising over them is that it rises above them, overcomes them and envelops them. Or, by way of metaphor, it reaches the sources that cause them.

Mu'sadah means closed, sealed shut. He said:

"My she-camel yearns for the mountains of Makkah, and between her and them are the gates of San'a, sealed shut."

[[He means: my she-camel yearns with longing for the mountains of Makkah, the plural of jabal, like asbab and sabab, because it is her homeland, while the gates of San'a, a city in Yemen, are sealed shut before her. The purpose is to grieve him and make him long for his homeland, and attributing the yearning to the she-camel is an exaggeration.]]

It is also read: fi 'amadin, with two dammas; 'umud, with a sukun on the mim; and 'amad, with two fathas. The meaning is that it confirms their despair of leaving and their certainty of eternal imprisonment, so the gates are sealed upon them and stretched over them as posts, to make doubly sure. It is permissible that the meaning is: the Fire is sealed over them, while they are bound in extended posts like the stocks in which thieves are fastened. [[Al-Sihah says: al-miqtarah is al-faliq, a wooden piece with holes into which the feet of prisoners are inserted. (Gh.)]] O Allah, protect us from the Fire, O best of those sought for protection.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Humazah, Allah will give him ten good deeds, equal to the number of those who mocked Muhammad and his Companions." [[Recorded by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]

[[He means: my she-camel yearns with longing for the mountains of Makkah, the plural of jabal, like asbab and sabab, because it is her homeland, while the gates of San'a, a city in Yemen, are sealed shut before her. The purpose is to grieve him and make him long for his homeland, and attributing the yearning to the she-camel is an exaggeration.]]

It is also read: fi 'amadin, with two dammas; 'umud, with a sukun on the mim; and 'amad, with two fathas. The meaning is that it confirms their despair of leaving and their certainty of eternal imprisonment, so the gates are sealed upon them and stretched over them as posts, to make doubly sure. It is permissible that the meaning is: the Fire is sealed over them, while they are bound in extended posts like the stocks in which thieves are fastened. [[Al-Sihah says: al-miqtarah is al-faliq, a wooden piece with holes into which the feet of prisoners are inserted. (Gh.)]] O Allah, protect us from the Fire, O best of those sought for protection.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Humazah, Allah will give him ten good deeds, equal to the number of those who mocked Muhammad and his Companions." [[Recorded by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 104, verses 1–9:

Makkan, and its verses are 9 [revealed after al-Qiyamah]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-hamz (the breaking, like al-hazm). Al-lamz is slandering. It is said: lamazahu and lahazahu, meaning he slandered him. The meaning is breaking people's honour, belittling them (ghadd minhum), backbiting them, and defaming them. [[The commentator's phrase "breaking people's honour and belittling them" is explained in al-Sihah: ghadda minhu means he lowered him, diminished him, and reduced his standing. (Gh.)]] [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning of al-humaza is one who frequently slanders people and disparages them..." Ahmad said: How excellent is the contrast between al-humaza al-lumaza and al-hutama. When He marked him with this trait in a form that indicates it is firmly rooted in him and entrenched in him, He followed the emphasis with His threat of the Fire, which He named al-Hutama because of what is cast into it. In specifying it He used an intensive form on the pattern of the form that contains the sin, so that there is equivalence between the sin and the recompense. Thus, the one who was accustomed to sin, his recompense is this al-Hutama, which is habitually crushing everything cast into it.]] The pattern fu'alah indicates that this is his habit, to which he has become accustomed. Similar are al-lu'nah (the curse) and al-du'hakah (the one who laughs much). He said:

"If I am absent, you are the one who slanders and backbites."

[[When you meet me, you grin at me from a distance, and when I am absent you are the backbiter who abundantly defames my honour.]]

This is by Ziyad al-A'jam. Al-shahth, with a fatha, means distance. Kathara 'an asnanihi means he showed his teeth in laughter and other things, but in the Arabic language this is known primarily for the first (laughter). Al-hamz is breaking, and al-lamz is slander. It is reported that a Bedouin was asked: "Does the mouse get broken (yahmizu)?" He said: "Yes, the cat breaks it," meaning it eats it. The al-hamiz here is the backbiter, the one who frequently backbites, who fills his mouth with what damages another's honour. Al-humazah is one who has made this a habit. Al-lamiz is one who attacks another with insults. Al-lumazah is one who has made this a habit. He means: when you meet me across the distance between us, you laugh at me, and when I am absent from you, you are the backbiter who abundantly defames my honour. It is also reported as "and if I am absent, you are the al-hamiz," in the passive form.

It is also read: "Woe to the al-humazah al-lumazah." And it is read: "Woe to every humazah lumazah," with a sukun on the mim, meaning the mocker who brings up outrageous things and jokes, so that he is laughed at and insulted. It is said that it was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose habit was backbiting and disparagement. It is said that it was about Umayyah ibn Khalaf. It is said that it was about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and his backbiting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and belittling him. It is permissible that the cause was specific while the threat is general, so that it encompasses everyone who engages in that ugly act, and so that it serves as an indirect rebuke to the one mentioned, since that is more effective in restraining him and more painful to him. Alladhi is a substitute for "every" (from kull), or it is in the accusative on the basis of censure. It is also read: jamma'a with the shaddah, which corresponds to his number. It is said 'addadahu means he made it a count for the calamities of time. It is also read: wa-'addadahu, meaning he gathered wealth, counted its amount and reckoned it. Or it means he gathered his wealth and the people who support him, from your saying: "So-and-so has a number and a band" when he has a large number of supporters and what they need. It is said that wa-'addadahu means wa-'adda-hu, with the idghām undone, like dannu akhlada-hu and khalladahu, which have the same meaning, meaning: wealth prolonged his hope, and far-reaching wishes gave him hope, until, because of his extreme heedlessness and long hope, he thinks his wealth has left him immortal in this world and that he will not die. Or it means he acts, through constructing buildings firmly with stone and brick, planting trees and cultivating the land, as one who thinks his wealth has kept him alive. Or it is an indirect reference to righteous deeds, and that it is these that cause their doer to abide in bliss, whereas wealth has not made anyone abide in anything.

It is reported that al-Akhnas had four thousand dinars. It is said ten thousand. From al-Hasan: he returned wealthy and said: "What do you say about thousands with which I did not ransom myself from a base person, nor did I show favour to a noble one?" He said: "But why?" He said: "Because of the calamity of the age, the harshness of the ruler, the misfortunes of time, and fear of poverty." He said: "Then you leave it to one who does not praise you, and you give back to one who does not excuse you."

Kalla (no indeed) is a rebuke to him for his assumption. It is read: la-yanbadhanna, meaning he and his wealth; la-yanbadhanna with the dhamma on the dhal, meaning he and his helpers. La-yanbadhanna fi al-hutamah, in the Fire, which by its nature crushes everything cast into it. It is said of a man who eats excessively: he is a hutamah. It is also read: al-hatimah, meaning that it enters their insides until it reaches their chests and rises over their hearts, which are the middle of the heart. Nothing in the human body is more delicate than the heart, and nothing more sensitive to pain from the slightest harm touching it. How much more so when the Fire of Hell rises over it and takes control of it. It is permissible that the hearts are singled out because they are the seats of disbelief, corrupt beliefs and evil intentions. The meaning of the Fire rising over them is that it rises above them, overcomes them and envelops them. Or, by way of metaphor, it reaches the sources that cause them.
